desc:
Consider the (n + 1) x (n + 1) grid of points whose coordinates run from 0 to n in each direction. Count the squares whose four corners are all points of this grid. Squares may be tilted, not only axis-aligned.

The count grows quickly, so return it modulo 1,000,000,007.

n = 1 -> 1    (the unit square)
n = 2 -> 6    (4 unit squares, 1 square of side 2, and 1 tilted square)
n = 3 -> 20
hints: Describe a square by one of its sides as a vector (a, b). Rotating the vector by 90 degrees gives the other sides, so each square has exactly one side vector with a > 0 and b ≥ 0.
A square with side vector (a, b) has a bounding box of size (a + b) x (a + b). How many positions can such a box take in the grid?
Group the vectors by s = a + b: there are s vectors with that sum, and the box fits in (n - s + 1)2 positions. Sum s * (n - s + 1)2 over s.
editorial: Every square has four side vectors obtained by rotating one of them by 90 degrees. Exactly one of the four lies in the half-open quadrant a > 0, b ≥ 0, so counting squares is the same as counting the vectors (a, b) in that quadrant together with a position for each.

A square with side vector (a, b) has a bounding box whose width and height are both a + b. The box has its lower-left corner at some point of the grid, and it fits in the grid for (n - (a + b) + 1)2 positions, provided a + b ≤ n.

For a fixed s = a + b there are s choices of a from 1 to s. The total is the sum of s * (n - s + 1)2 over s = 1..n, an O(n) loop. The brute force that tries every four-point subset agrees with it on small n.
